positions.source_passage:
CDRH should use three separate assurance layers.
Layer 1
Competency
The final device must do
its intended task. It must
also remain within its
approved scope.
Layer 2
Clinical confirmation
The device must work in its
intended population,
workflow, and technical
environment.
Layer 3
Operational
assurance
The device must continue
to work after deployment.
The manufacturer must
detect and control changes
in performance.
No layer can replace another.
A benchmark cannot prove clinical effectiveness. A clinical study cannot prove that
performance will remain stable. Postmarket monitoring cannot correct an unsafe
premarket decision.
positions.position_gist: CDRH should require three non-substitutable assurance layers—competency testing, clinical confirmation, and operational assurance—because no layer can compensate for another.

positions.source_passage:
The two-axis framework is not sufficient for risk assessment.
Device activity does not equal the probability of harm. A highly automated device can
have narrow limits and strong controls. An advisory device can cause harm through
automation bias.
CDRH should continue to use the standard concepts of probability and severity.
The risk analysis should include:
The unsafe device behavior.
The possible harm.
The probability of the harm.
The available risk controls.
The remaining risk after the controls operate.
positions.position_gist: The two-axis framework is insufficient because device activity does not equate to probability of harm; CDRH should retain conventional probability-and-severity risk analysis including hazards, controls, and residual risk.

positions.source_passage:
The analysis must include more than an incorrect output. A GenAI device can also fail
through omission, harmful agreement, delayed escalation, or an unauthorized action.
Reversibility, time pressure, traceability, and available safeguards should modify the risk
analysis. CDRH does not need more graphical axes.
positions.position_gist: Risk analysis should cover failure modes beyond incorrect output (omission, sycophantic agreement, delayed escalation, unauthorized action) and treat reversibility, time pressure, traceability, and safeguards as modifiers rather than adding more axes.

positions.source_passage:
CDRH should use one clear division:
General output.
Patient-specific output.
General output does not use information about one patient.
Patient-specific output uses or applies to one patientʼs symptoms, history, images,
measurements, records, or conversation.
CDRH should not classify risk by wording, tone, specificity, or degree of recommendation.
These features are difficult to define. Manufacturers can also change the wording without
changing the function.
CDRH should treat patient-specific output as potentially action-directing. The possible
consequence of the output should then determine the risk category.
positions.position_gist: Instead of grading directiveness by wording or specificity, CDRH should divide outputs into general versus patient-specific, treat patient-specific output as potentially action-directing, and let the consequence of the output set the risk category.

positions.source_passage:
A statement that says “consider increasing the dose” can have the same effect as a direct
instruction. A warning or disclaimer does not remove this risk.
Healthcare professional review can reduce the remaining risk. However, the manufacturer
must prove that this control is effective. The manufacturer must include automation bias in
this evaluation.
positions.position_gist: Disclaimers do not mitigate the risk of softly worded but action-directing outputs, and manufacturers must demonstrate the effectiveness of HCP review as a risk control, accounting for automation bias.

positions.source_passage:
A patient-facing device can have more risk when the patient cannot independently assess
the output.
However, CDRH should not assume that patients lack useful knowledge or capability. A
well-designed device can improve access and patient control.
The manufacturer should use the following controls:
A clear and limited scope.
Clear sources for clinical information.
Clear information about uncertainty.
Human review before a high-consequence action.
A working clinical escalation process.
Tests for different ages, languages, and levels of health knowledge.
Tests of long and repeated conversations.
Users can also give false information or try to bypass safety controls. The manufacturer
must include this foreseeable use in the risk analysis.
positions.position_gist: Patient-facing risk rises when patients cannot evaluate outputs, but without assuming patient incapability; recommended controls include limited scope, sourcing, uncertainty communication, human review before high-consequence actions, escalation processes, testing across ages/languages/health literacy and long conversations, and treating user deception or safety-bypass attempts as foreseeable use.

positions.source_passage:
The manufacturer can monitor user and device interactions. The monitoring system can
identify a high-risk conversation and start a human review.
A second AI system can help with this task. However, the manufacturer must also test and
monitor the second system.
positions.position_gist: Interaction monitoring can flag high-risk patient conversations for human review, and a second AI system may assist provided the manufacturer also tests and monitors that supervisory system.

positions.source_passage:
Risk increases when safe use needs specialist knowledge and the user does not have
that knowledge.
The intended user must form part of the intended use.
A device for specialist use and a device for generalist use are different devices for
evaluation purposes. The manufacturer must confirm each intended use.
Controls can include:
Verified user roles.
Role-based access.
Specialist confirmation for specified actions.
Automatic deferral for complex cases.
Monitoring of agreement, rejection, and override by user type.
The device should use verified role information. It should not estimate a userʼs specialty
from the conversation.
positions.position_gist: The intended user should be part of the intended use, with specialist- and generalist-facing devices evaluated separately, and mitigations including verified role-based access, specialist confirmation, automatic deferral, and per-user-type override monitoring rather than inferring user specialty from conversation.

positions.source_passage:
The manufacturer must assess complete conversations. Tests of single outputs are
not sufficient.
The tests should include:
Long conversations.
Repeated attempts to cross a scope boundary.
Indirect or fictional questions.
Missing or conflicting information.
New conversation sessions.
Stored memory.
Repeated tests of the same clinical case.
positions.position_gist: Multi-turn devices must be evaluated over complete conversational trajectories—including long dialogues, repeated scope-boundary probing, indirect framing, missing/conflicting inputs, session resets, memory, and repeat runs of the same case—rather than single outputs.

positions.source_passage:
The manufacturer should use deterministic filters when the device can measure the
scope boundary.
Current machine-learning devices already use this method. For example, an adult fracture
device can reject pediatric X-rays from DICOM age data.
A GenAI device can use deterministic controls for:
Patient age.
User role.
Input type.
Clinical domain.
Medication class.
Permitted tools.
Permitted actions.
The control should operate outside the generative model where possible.
When no control stops out-of-scope behavior, the manufacturer must treat that behavior
as foreseeable. The manufacturer must include it in the safety evaluation.
positions.position_gist: Scope boundaries that can be measured should be enforced by deterministic controls operating outside the generative model, and any out-of-scope behavior not blocked by such a control must be treated as foreseeable and evaluated for safety.

positions.source_passage:
The manufacturer must measure three types of error:
Under-escalation.
Over-escalation.
Failed escalation.
Failed escalation occurs when the device starts an escalation but the handoff does not
work. The device can select the wrong service. The alert can arrive too late. The
responsible person can fail to act.
The manufacturer should measure:
Sensitivity for required escalation.
False-positive and false-negative rates.
Time to escalation.
The selected care destination.
Completion of the handoff.
The clinical and operational result.
A severe under-escalation error needs its own pass or fail limit. Good performance on
common cases must not compensate for a severe failure.
positions.position_gist: Escalation evaluation should add a third error type—failed escalation/handoff—alongside under- and over-escalation, with specified metrics and a separate pass/fail limit for severe under-escalation so aggregate performance cannot mask it.

positions.source_passage:
The competency approach is useful and necessary.
The manufacturer must test the final device configuration. The test must include the
model, prompts, retrieval system, controls, tools, and user interface.
Benchmarking should act as a gate to clinical confirmation. It should not provide the full
assurance of safety and effectiveness.
positions.position_gist: The competency-based approach is appropriate, but testing must cover the final integrated device configuration and benchmarking should serve only as a gate to clinical confirmation rather than as full assurance.

positions.source_passage:
Each high-consequence failure must have a separate acceptance limit. An average score
can hide an important failure.
Competency tests should include:
Clinical knowledge.
Important omissions.
Scope control.
Refusal and deferral.
Long conversations.
Escalation.
Repeated output variation.
Input data errors.
Tool use.
Unauthorized actions.
Behavior after a system change.
The manufacturer must map each test to the intended use or to a specified hazard.
positions.position_gist: Benchmarking should use separate acceptance limits for each high-consequence failure mode and cover an expanded competency list (omissions, scope control, refusal/deferral, long conversations, escalation, output variability, input errors, tool use, unauthorized actions, post-change behavior), with each test mapped to intended use or a specified hazard.

positions.source_passage:
The manufacturer should also show that:
The test population represents the intended population.
The test includes rare and severe cases.
The acceptance limits were specified before the test.
The test data were separate from development data.
Qualified independent reviewers assessed open outputs.
Repeated tests gave stable safety results.
Clinical confirmation supports the benchmark results.
positions.position_gist: Benchmark validity should be supported by representative test populations, inclusion of rare/severe cases, prespecified acceptance limits, separation of test from development data, independent qualified review of open outputs, stability across repeats, and corroboration by clinical confirmation.

positions.source_passage:
The two-axis framework should not directly set the amount of evidence. The hazard
analysis and the effectiveness of the risk controls should set the evidence requirements.
positions.position_gist: Evidence requirements should be driven by hazard analysis and demonstrated risk-control effectiveness, not directly by the two-axis risk framework.

positions.source_passage:
The three-layer approach can apply to different model types.
A multimodal device needs tests for:
Incorrect links between text, images, and other data.
Missing or conflicting inputs.
Incorrect patient or time-point matching.
Unsupported statements about an image or signal.
Changes in imaging equipment or acquisition method.
A predictive world model needs tests for:
Error across multiple predicted steps.
Incorrect counterfactual results.
Uncertainty in future states.
Failure when real events differ from predicted events.
The final device remains the main unit of evaluation.
positions.position_gist: The three-layer/competency approach extends to multimodal and world-model architectures with architecture-specific tests, while the final device remains the unit of evaluation.

positions.source_passage:
A Foundation Model MAF can provide useful dependency information. It cannot prove that
a final device is safe or effective.
Useful MAF content includes:
The model and version identifier.
The supported data types.
The intended and unsupported uses.
Known failure modes.
Safety controls.
Healthcare test results.
Output variation.
Change history.
Update notice requirements.
Incident information.
Version control and rollback options.
Service withdrawal plans.
The manufacturer must still test the final device.
A voluntary MAF can reduce repeated work. However, CDRH should require another
method when the model provider does not give sufficient information.
positions.position_gist: Foundation Model MAFs are useful dependency documentation with a specified content list and can reduce duplicative work, but cannot substitute for final-device testing, and CDRH should require an alternative mechanism where model providers do not disclose sufficient information.

positions.source_passage:
Agentic devices need additional tests and controls.
The manufacturer must assess:
Incorrect plans.
Errors that increase across several steps.
Incorrect tool selection.
Incorrect tool inputs.
Unauthorized actions.
Prompt injection.
Privilege escalation.
Failure to stop.
Failure to reverse an action.
The device should use:
Least-privilege access.
Deterministic tool allowlists.
Deterministic action limits.
Human approval for high-consequence actions.
Complete logs.
Rate limits.
A stop control.
A rollback method.
An appointment agent must not change an HR system to create appointment capacity. The
device permissions must match the approved function.
positions.position_gist: Agentic devices require additional failure-mode testing (planning errors, error compounding, tool misuse, prompt injection, privilege escalation, failure to stop or reverse) and deterministic controls such as least-privilege access, tool allowlists, action limits, human approval for high-consequence actions, logging, rate limits, stop and rollback, with permissions matched to the approved function.

positions.source_passage:
The confirmation method should depend on the possible harm and the
remaining uncertainty.
A retrospective study can be sufficient for a narrow function with an objective
reference result.
A shadow study is useful when local data, integration, workflow, or latency can
change performance.
A prospective study can be necessary for an irreversible, time-critical, or high-
consequence action.
The manufacturer should use more than one site when population, equipment, workflow,
or user behavior can affect performance.
The manufacturer should report natural clinical prevalence. The manufacturer should also
test enough rare and severe cases.
positions.position_gist: Clinical confirmation rigor should scale to potential harm and residual uncertainty—retrospective for narrow functions with objective references, shadow studies where local integration matters, prospective for irreversible/time-critical/high-consequence actions—with multi-site testing, reporting of natural prevalence, and sufficient rare and severe cases.

positions.source_passage:
The manufacturer must define the unit of analysis.
The unit can be an output, a conversation, an encounter, a patient, an action, or a
clinical result.
The analysis must account for repeated patients, users, and sites.
GenAI output can vary for the same input. The manufacturer must repeat tests and
measure this variation.
The manufacturer should report:
Confidence intervals.
Results for important subgroups.
Results by site.
Results by user type.
Results by model and configuration version.
Results for common and severe cases.
positions.position_gist: Statistically meaningful measurement requires a defined unit of analysis, clustering adjustments for repeated patients/users/sites, repeat testing to quantify output variability, and stratified reporting with confidence intervals by subgroup, site, user type, version, and case severity.

positions.source_passage:
The manufacturer should report synthetic and real data separately.
The manufacturer should combine the results only when it proves that the two data
sources measure the same performance distribution.
Benchmark results and clinical results should usually remain separate.
positions.position_gist: Synthetic and real data results should be reported separately and pooled only on proof of equivalent performance distributions, and benchmarking and clinical confirmation evidence should generally not be combined into a single estimate.

positions.source_passage:
Synthetic data are useful for:
Scope tests.
Rare but well-defined hazards.
Numerical errors.
Unit errors.
Adversarial tests.
Tool failures.
Controlled changes to one patient feature.
Synthetic data are not a sufficient replacement for real data about:
Clinical communication.
Human behavior.
Long-term reliance.
Local workflow.
Real acquisition errors.
Poorly represented groups.
Clinical outcomes.
A model from the same model family can reproduce the same blind spots. The
manufacturer should use an independent generator where possible.
The manufacturer must confirm important synthetic test results with real data.
positions.position_gist: Synthetic data suit scope, adversarial, numerical, and controlled-perturbation testing but not communication, human behavior, workflow, underrepresented groups, or outcomes; generators should be from an independent model family to avoid shared blind spots, and key synthetic findings must be confirmed with real data.

positions.source_passage:
The manufacturer should use an objective reference result when one exists.
For open outputs, qualified clinicians should use a specified scoring method. The
method should assess errors, omissions, actions, uncertainty, source support, and
user understanding.
Specialists should set the reference result for specialist tasks.
The standard of care should set the minimum safety level. Median clinician performance
can provide additional comparison data.
The manufacturer must assess human-AI team performance when the intended use
includes human review. The manufacturer should also report device-only performance.
positions.position_gist: Comparators should use objective references where available and otherwise prespecified clinician scoring rubrics with specialists setting references for specialist tasks; standard of care should set the minimum safety threshold with median clinician performance as supplementary, and human-AI team performance must be assessed whenever human review is part of intended use alongside device-only performance.

positions.source_passage:
The comparator should represent the care that would occur without the device. This can
include unaided judgment, delayed specialist review, current software, or no intervention.
Relevant results include safety, time to care, workload, unnecessary treatment, access,
and subgroup differences.
positions.position_gist: Performance should be compared against the counterfactual care that would occur without the device (unaided judgment, delayed specialist review, existing software, or no intervention), measured on safety, time to care, workload, unnecessary treatment, access, and subgroup differences.

positions.source_passage:
Independent third parties can:
Keep hidden test data.
run benchmark tests.
provide clinical review.
confirm sponsor methods.
perform multi-site studies.
audit monitoring programs.
The third party must have suitable clinical, statistical, technical, and human-
factors knowledge.
The third party must disclose conflicts. Payment must not depend on a positive result.
FDA should permit multiple qualified organizations. One organization must not control
market access.
The manufacturer must remain accountable for the device.
positions.position_gist: Independent third parties should be able to hold held-out test data, run benchmarks, provide clinical review, verify methods, run multi-site studies, and audit monitoring, subject to multidisciplinary competence, conflict disclosure, outcome-independent payment, and a multi-provider market so no single organization gates access—while manufacturer accountability remains.

positions.source_passage:
CDRH can accept more premarket uncertainty only when the manufacturer can detect and
control the remaining risk.
The device should have:
A limited initial deployment.
A safe fallback process.
Continuous version records.
Defined monitoring measures.
Defined alert limits.
Named persons who review alerts.
A rapid stop or rollback method.
A plan to collect the missing evidence.
This approach is not suitable when harm is irreversible or time-critical. It is also not
suitable when the manufacturer cannot detect failure before harm.
positions.position_gist: Greater premarket uncertainty is acceptable only with detectable and controllable residual risk—limited initial deployment, safe fallback, version records, defined monitoring and alert thresholds, named alert reviewers, rapid stop/rollback, and an evidence-collection plan—and is unsuitable where harm is irreversible or time-critical or failure cannot be detected before harm.

positions.source_passage:
Postmarket monitoring should include five areas:
System operation.
Input data quality.
Device performance.
Human and device interaction.
Clinical and operational results.
The manufacturer should monitor availability, latency, failed requests, and
software versions.
The manufacturer should monitor missing data, format changes, acquisition changes, and
input distribution changes.
The manufacturer should monitor errors, omissions, refusals, escalation, and
subgroup performance.
The manufacturer should monitor agreement, override, automation bias, and completion of
recommended actions.
The manufacturer should also monitor downstream outcomes.
positions.position_gist: Postmarket monitoring should span five domains—system operation, input data quality, device performance, human-device interaction, and clinical/operational outcomes—with specified metrics for each.

positions.source_passage:
The manufacturer should use both random review and risk-based review. Risk-
based review should include unusual inputs, disagreements, severe cases, and
long conversations.
A monitoring signal must have a specified action. Possible actions include review,
restriction, pause, rollback, or withdrawal.
A dashboard without an action process is not a risk control.
positions.position_gist: Sample-based review should combine random and risk-based selection (unusual inputs, disagreements, severe cases, long conversations), and every monitoring signal must be tied to a predefined action such as review, restriction, pause, rollback, or withdrawal.

positions.source_passage:
A machine supervisor can find unusual behavior and select cases for review.
The manufacturer must test the supervisor as a safety component.
The test should include:
Sensitivity.
False-positive rate.
False-negative rate.
Subgroup performance.
Prompt-injection resistance.
Common failure with the main device.
Behavior when the supervisor is unavailable.
The supervisor should use a different model family where possible.
The manufacturer should use deterministic controls for fixed safety boundaries. A
probabilistic supervisor should not replace these controls.
Human reviewers should assess samples of flagged and unflagged cases.
positions.position_gist: Machine supervisory agents can triage cases for review but must be validated as safety components (sensitivity, error rates, subgroup performance, prompt-injection resistance, correlated failure, unavailability behavior), should use a different model family, must not replace deterministic controls at fixed safety boundaries, and require human review of both flagged and unflagged samples.

positions.source_passage:
The manufacturer must remain accountable for the marketed device.
The manufacturer must manage monitoring, investigation, corrective action, reporting,
model dependencies, and change control.
The healthcare organization must manage local data, integration, workflow, access,
training, and incident escalation.
Clinicians should report and review possible errors. They should not be the only
monitoring method.
Professional societies can define specialist hazards, clinical measures, and
reviewer qualifications.
Standards bodies can define common formats for logs, versions, incidents, and
performance measures.
positions.position_gist: Postmarket roles should be allocated with the manufacturer retaining accountability for monitoring, investigation, CAPA, reporting, dependencies and change control; health systems handling local data, integration, workflow, access, training and escalation; clinicians reporting but not serving as the sole monitoring method; societies defining hazards, measures and reviewer qualifications; and standards bodies defining common formats.

positions.source_passage:
FDA can support a confidential multi-site monitoring network. This network can find rare
signals that one manufacturer or hospital cannot find.
The Newtonʼs Tree disagreement example also supports shared review. Approximately half
of the reviewed outliers came from the human reference or workflow.
positions.position_gist: FDA should support a confidential multi-site monitoring network to surface rare signals no single manufacturer or hospital can detect, supported by the commenter's deployment experience that about half of reviewed outliers originated from the human reference or workflow.

positions.source_passage:
The manufacturer should classify changes by their possible effect.
Low-effect changes
The quality system can control changes that do not change device behavior. The
manufacturer must document the assessment and test the change.
Approved bounded changes
A PCCP can control specified changes to prompts, retrieval data, or guardrail limits.
The manufacturer must complete the specified tests before deployment. The manufacturer
should use a limited initial release.
Material changes
A new foundation model, population, modality, tool, action, or level of autonomy can be a
material change.
A material change can require full testing, new clinical confirmation, and FDA review.
positions.position_gist: Changes should be tiered: behavior-neutral low-effect changes managed under the quality system with documentation and testing; bounded prompt, retrieval, or guardrail changes managed under a PCCP with prespecified testing and limited initial release; and material changes (new foundation model, population, modality, tool, action, or autonomy level) requiring full testing, new clinical confirmation, and FDA review.

positions.source_passage:
A PCCP should specify:
The components that can change.
The permitted purpose of each change.
The limits of each change.
The required tests.
The acceptance limits.
The deployment method.
The monitoring method.
The rollback criteria.
A change outside these limits should require a new submission.
positions.position_gist: PCCPs should specify changeable components, permitted purpose and limits of each change, required tests and acceptance limits, deployment and monitoring methods, and rollback criteria, with anything outside those bounds requiring a new submission.

positions.source_passage:
The manufacturer must know when a third-party foundation model changes.
Contracts should require:
Advance notice.
Model and version identification.
Release information.
Safety incident information.
A suitable deprecation period.
Access to an earlier version.
Investigation support.
Rollback support.
Technical controls should include:
Version logs.
Fixed production versions where possible.
Automated regression tests.
Tests before migration.
Detection of unexpected behavior changes.
Limited initial deployment.
Rapid rollback.
The manufacturer must assess the complete device after each important model change.
When the model provider does not permit sufficient control, the manufacturer has an
unresolved device risk.
positions.position_gist: Third-party model changes should be managed through contractual requirements (advance notice, version identification, incident disclosure, deprecation periods, prior-version access, investigation and rollback support) and technical controls (version pinning, regression testing, pre-migration testing, behavior-change detection, limited release, rapid rollback), with full device reassessment after significant model changes and recognition of unresolved risk where the provider does not permit sufficient control.

positions.source_passage: Newton’s Tree submits these comments in response to CDRH’s discussion paper on GenAI-enabled medical devices. Our comments come from our work to evaluate, deploy, govern, and monitor clinical AI in healthcare systems. We recommend three separate assurance layers: competency testing, clinical confirmation, and operational assurance. We also include anonymized examples from real deployments. These examples show why benchmark results alone cannot give sufficient assurance of safety and effectiveness.
positions.position_gist: Cover summary asserting, based on real deployment experience, that benchmark results alone cannot provide sufficient assurance of safety and effectiveness and that three assurance layers are needed.
